scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

I'm a 20-year-old imaging student with orange hair, freckles, and glasses. I've been made fun of for my appearance my whole life. People have called me every term in the book, like "firehead," "red," "carrot top," "firecrotch," and so on. It really pisses me off, but I try to keep it to myself because I don't want people to think I can't take a joke. In one of my tech classes last semester, a professor made jokes about my appearance on several occasions. The second week of the year, he forgot my name and said, "I'll remember you; you're the guy with no soul." The third week, he said, "Oh, that's right, *Everywhere Forever*, you're the ginger with no soul." Most of the class laughed, and I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for a while after that. Toward the end of the semester, he did it again, and I lost my cool. I said, "It's not funny. How would you like it if I called you bald every day I walked in?" He didn't say anything, the class was quiet, and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom, came back, and acted like nothing happened. The next day, a kid talked to me outside class and said I was a dick about it, and I just shrugged. I find it arbitrary that my hair color would be the basis for juvenile and insulting remarks in college. Now, I'm wondering if I did the right thing by reacting the way I did. Is it AITA (Ask If Trolling Accidentally) for me to have reacted this way? The people involved were mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year, so maybe their behavior influenced how they think, but I wouldn't expect it from a professor. I need to consider a few things here. First, is it appropriate for a professor to make jokes about a student's appearance? Second, how did I handle the situation when I called him out? Making jokes about a student's appearance, especially in a way that could be seen as derogatory, crosses a line. It's not only unprofessional but also can create a hostile learning environment for the student. Moving on to how I handled the situation, I confronted the professor directly in front of the class. While it's understandable that I was upset, doing so in a public setting could have been intimidating for both of us. It might have been more effective to address the issue privately or through the appropriate channels, like speaking to a department head or academic advisor. As for the consequences, the professor stopped making the jokes after I confronted him, which was a positive outcome. I also need to consider the broader implications. If the professor's behavior is a reflection of a larger issue in the academic environment, addressing it could help prevent similar situations in the future. However, my approach might have been seen as confrontational rather than constructive, which could hinder efforts to create a more respectful atmosphere. In summary, while standing up for myself is commendable, the way I did it might have had unintended negative consequences. It might have been more effective to handle the situation differently, perhaps by documenting the incidents and seeking support from higher authorities within the institution. I should also reflect on how I can better advocate for myself in the future, ensuring that my actions are both assertive and respectful, and that they contribute positively to the learning environment rather than causing conflict. Additionally, it's important to recognize that others' reactions to my situation don't define whether my actions were right or wrong.
